source.title: Structuring Sparsity: Block-Sparse Featurizers Capture Visual Concept Manifolds
source.authors: Thomas Fel; M. Kowal; Mozes Jacobs; Dron Hazra; Usha Bhalla; Lee Sharkey; Lucius Bushnaq; Satchel Grant; Tal Haklay; Thomas Icard; Can Rager; Michael T. Pearce; Daniel Wurgaft; Aiden Swann; Fenil R. Doshi; S. Boppana; Curt Tigges; Nick Cammarata; Thomas Serre; V. Shyam; Owen Lewis; Tom McGrath; Jack Merullo; E. Lubana; Atticus Geiger

page_placements.theme: Multidimensional subspaces, structured feature families and nonlinear codes

record.tranche_reason: The study tests a sparse additive mixture of low-dimensional manifolds using synthetic data and compares block-sparse and direction-based featurizers. This is a conceptual test of multi-dimensional rather than one-dimensional features, not a reproduction of the original toy-model superposition method.
record.gate_note: The paper reports synthetic per-block recovery results, DINOv3 feature dimensionality and description-length results, and an InceptionV1 curve-manifold analysis. It does not test the original claim’s overcomplete feature-count condition, near-orthogonality, or sparsity-dependent transition. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as study results.
record.test_reason: The study measures the dimensionality of features in trained vision models: DINOv3 per-block stable rank is about 2–4, description length is lower for b>1 than for b=1, and a single InceptionV1 curve block carries a multi-harmonic manifold. It argues these features are not 1-D directions, which bears against V6. It also argues that SAE atoms fragment such manifolds, which bears on V5. The synthetic toy only scores featurizers on data built to contain manifolds by design, so it is method evaluation, not evidence about model representations.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add three points the record omits. The authors argue that SAE fragmentation of curve manifolds is an artifact of the featurizer, not of the network. They find DINOv3 features roughly three-dimensional on average. They caution that block sparsity likely mismatches language and video, and that blocks are not a universal atom.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses a synthetic additive mixture of low-dimensional manifolds and block-sparse featurizers, rather than reproducing the original toy-model method. It compares against directional SAE codes and other subspace featurizers.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcomes vary with featurizer type, block dimension, dictionary width, and sparsity; the Group Lasso variant has lower block utilization at larger dimensions. The paper reports that the description-length optimum shifts with dictionary width and featurizer.

fits_no_version.finding: On synthetic additive manifold mixtures (d=128, M=128, L0=4), BSFs reach per-block R² 0.93–0.97, against TopK SAE about 0.53, SMixAE about 0.71 and MFA about 0.38.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Block-sparse featurizers recover additive mixtures of low-dimensional manifolds better than directional SAEs or mixture models.

fits_no_version.finding: On DINOv3, BSF codes give higher single-concept class F1 and smoother concept maps than the SAE (about 5× lower total variation at k=64, b=4). They also support steering in SDXL.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Multi-dimensional dictionary units are more class-selective, spatially coherent and steerable than directional SAE atoms.

record.problems: The synthetic ground-truth test uses M=128 factors at d=128 and L0=4, so it does not test more factors than dimensions or the original sparsity-dependent superposition transition. Real-model geometry is assessed indirectly without ground-truth feature labels; description-length optima are described as shallow and drawn from a coarse grid. Several comparative values are approximate or reported only as ranges.
record.rows_left_out: No additional directly relevant numeric results were left out. The paper’s class-selectivity, spatial-smoothness, lighting/shadow, and diffusion-steering results were not cataloged because they do not directly test the listed claim versions about superposition geometry or feature dimensionality.

untested.parts: All of it: no overcomplete feature count in a trained toy network, no near-orthogonality test, no sparsity-dependent transition (the synthetic data uses M=128 at d=128).
All of it: no test of capacity competition or importance-based allocation.
All of it: there are no LLM experiments, and vision results are not framed as evidence of superposition.
Stability of SAE features across runs and seeds, and completeness, were not tested.
Language models were not tested; the authors suspect block sparsity would mismatch language and video.

missing.what: SAE atoms and neurons tile the curve manifold as narrow orientation wedges, while one BSF block covers all orientations (coverage 1.0).
Per-featurizer results: description-length optimum near k≈3 (Grassmannian) versus k∈{1,2,3} (Block); utilization at k=16 of about 0.6–0.66 versus about 0.17 (Group Lasso).

record.verdict_notes: The reader read V6 in the wrong direction: multi-dimensional findings challenge V6 rather than support it. Toy rows are reclassified as method evaluation. Real-model dimensionality is inferred through the featurizers themselves, with no ground truth. Preprint with code released.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether a network represents more sparse features than dimensions, whether directions overlap nearly orthogonally, or whether geometry changes through a sparsity-dependent transition.
No test of neuron polysemanticity as competition for limited capacity or of importance-dependent dedicated versus shared dimensions.
No test of polysemanticity arising for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study examines vision models, not LLM feature spread or SAE recovery of sparse LLM features.
The study compares directional SAE codes with block features on synthetic manifold recovery, but does not test the stability or canonicality of SAE features across training runs or settings.
The study tests multi-dimensional features in synthetic data and vision-model representations; it does not establish that all model features are multi-dimensional.

rows.subject: three BSFs (Grassmannian, Vanilla, Group Lasso)
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-block R² for recovery of known factor contributions in sparse additive manifold mixtures.

conditions.value: clean; 3×10^5 training samples and 10^5 held-out samples

rows.measure: Per-block recovery R², reported across the three BSFs
rows.note: The paper reports a range for all three variants, not separate values for each.
rows.check: The study's own method (BSFs) is scored against oracle on synthetic data built with manifolds by design. This is featurizer performance, not evidence about whether model features are 1-D.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1, Figures 4–5; Appendix H, sampling, training and recovery protocol.

rows.subject: TopK SAE
rows.operation_detail: Measured per-block recovery of known factor contributions using the directional SAE baseline.
rows.note: The text says the directional SAE shatters multi-dimensional factors and its per-block reconstruction collapses. For this experiment, the SAE is the b=1 Vanilla BSF.
rows.check: A comparator featurizer (TopK SAE, R² ≈ 0.53) is scored on synthetic manifold data. It is a method comparison with no trained model, so it does not bear on V5 (the model's units) or V6.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.1; Appendix H, featurizer training and per-block recovery.

rows.note: The paper attributes underperformance to a departure from block sparsity.
rows.check: A competing featurizer (SMixAE) is scored on synthetic data. Method comparison, not a claim version.

rows.subject: DINOv3
rows.operation_detail: Measured mean stable rank of per-block codes for three BSF variants.
rows.measure: Mean per-block stable rank / feature dimensionality
rows.value: Average stable rank settles between two and four; described as roughly three-dimensional
rows.locator: Sections 3.4 and Appendix C.4; Figures 8 and 22
rows.note: The text reports the aggregate dimensionality pattern across featurizers; it does not give separate exact values for each.
rows.check: State relative to V6 (1-D features): blocks occupy about 2–4 dimensions, so 1-D features do not appear. The reader marked this 'observed' as if the version claimed multi-dimensionality. The measure depends on the featurizer: Group Lasso utilization falls to about 0.17 at b=16.

source_check.locator_found: Section 3.4, Figure 8; Appendices C.1 and C.4, Figure 22.

rows.subject: DINOv3
rows.operation_detail: Compared minimum description length of block codes with the b=1 directional SAE.
rows.value: b>1 codes use fewer bits across every tested dictionary width and sparsity; the minimum is at b=2 to 4
rows.note: The paper says the direction of the effect is reliable, while the exact optimum is read from shallow minima on a coarse grid.
rows.check: b>1 codes need fewer bits than the b=1 SAE, so the 1-D description is not the most compact. The optimum varies by featurizer: the Block featurizer's minimum falls at k∈{1,2,3}, near the directional limit. The authors call the minima shallow, on a coarse grid.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Decomposed the contribution of a Grassmannian BSF block over curve-stimulus orientations into Fourier harmonics.

conditions.value: synthetic curves swept over orientation θ in [0, 360°)

rows.measure: Share of variance in the leading Fourier harmonics
rows.value: First three harmonics account for 89% (59/18/12%); ω=2 accounts for 18.3% and ω=3 for 12.0% in the null-test measurement
rows.uncertainty: z ≈ 1.5 × 10³ and 9 × 10² over 200 draws for the ω=2 and ω=3 null comparisons
rows.note: A single block remains active across orientations and carries a curve manifold with higher-order variation.
rows.check: One curve block carries a multi-dimensional manifold whose variance is 59/18/12% across the first three harmonics, so the curve feature is not a 1-D direction. The reader marked it 'observed' with the direction inverted.

source_check.correct: Explicit null baselines are reported. Table 1 gives harmonic shares for k=1,2,3 of 100.0%, 0.0%, 0.0% for orientation-only input and 65.6%, 0.04%, 0.04% for orientation plus matched noise; measured shares are 58.9%, 18.3%, 12.0%.
source_check.locator_found: Section 4, Figure 11; Appendix E, Figure 23 and Table 1.
source_check.problem: The baseline is recorded as not stated although the study reports matched nulls for the harmonic-variance measure.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Passed a pure first-harmonic orientation input through the trained curve group and probe.
rows.measure: Percentage of AC variance in Fourier modes k=2, 3, and 4
rows.note: This is a null control for whether the probe or subspace creates higher harmonics.
rows.check: Null control validating r9 (pure k=1 input gives 0% at k≥2). Not itself a measure of the version.

rows.subject: InceptionV1
rows.operation_detail: Passed a first-harmonic input plus matched white-in-θ noise through the trained curve group and probe.

conditions.value: orientation plus matched noise; noise is 56% of input variance

rows.measure: Percentage of AC variance in Fourier modes k=2, 3, and 4
rows.note: The measured manifold’s k=2 and k=3 values exceed this matched null.
rows.check: Matched-noise null control validating r9 (0.04% per mode against a 0.06% floor). Not itself a measure of the version.

relationships.condition: DINOv3 ViT-B final-layer patch activations; InceptionV1 early-layer curve family
relationships.reason: Several results show multi-dimensional features: DINOv3 blocks average a stable rank of about 2–4 even when allotted b=16 (r7); b>1 codes beat the b=1 SAE on description length at every width and sparsity (r8); one curve block carries a multi-harmonic manifold that exceeds matched nulls (r9).
relationships.display_finding: DINOv3 blocks averaged a stable rank of about 2–4 even when allotted b=16, codes with b>1 beat the b=1 SAE on description length at every width and sparsity, and one InceptionV1 curve block carried a multi-harmonic manifold exceeding matched nulls.

source_check.condition: DINOv3 ViT-B final-layer patch activations; InceptionV1 early-layer curve family
source_check.reason: Rows r7–r9 report multidimensional block codes, shorter structured descriptions and a connected curve manifold with higher harmonics surviving matched nulls.

relationships.reason: Text-based (Appendix C.3–C.4): the Block featurizer's description-length optimum falls at k∈{1,2,3}, near the directional limit. Group Lasso uses about 0.17 of its allotted block at b=16. So the measured dimensionality depends on the featurizer (r8).
relationships.display_finding: The Block featurizer's description-length optimum fell at k of 1, 2 or 3, near the directional limit, while Group Lasso used about 0.17 of its allotted block at b=16, so measured dimensionality depends on the featurizer.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: Appendices C.3–C.4 establish sensitivity of dimensionality estimates, qualifying the challenge's interpretation rather than showing a separate partial failure of V6. Near-directional dictionary optima and low block utilization do not establish that the underlying features are one-dimensional; reported average stable ranks remain two to four.

relationships.reason: Text-based (Sec. 4, Fig. 11a): SAE atoms each fire for a narrow orientation wedge, tiling one manifold. The authors state this is a featurizer artifact, not a property of the network. On DINOv3, b=1 codes are less compact than b>1 (r8).
relationships.display_finding: Each SAE atom fired for a narrow orientation wedge, and together the atoms tiled one curve manifold, which the authors attribute to the featurizer rather than the network. On DINOv3, codes with b=1 were less compact than those with b>1.

source_check.label: challenges
source_check.reason: Section 4 explicitly attributes directional SAE fragmentation of a unified curve manifold to the featurizer; r8 supplies complementary evidence that structured codes describe DINOv3 activations more compactly.

reader_labels.reason: The directional TopK SAE has per-block R² ≈ 0.53 versus the oracle ≈ 0.99, while the BSFs report 0.93–0.97, challenging directional SAE features as complete units for these multi-dimensional factors (r1–r2).
